Linear homogeneous differential equation of order n.

We will consider linear homogeneous differential equation of order n

                 a0(x)y (n)(x) + a1(x)y (n−1)(x) + ... + an−1(x)y ′(x) + an(x)y(x) = 0,              (1)

where a0, a1, ..., an are continuous functions on interval I and that a0(x) ̸= 0 for any x ∈I.
From Existence and uniqueness theorem it follows that there exists a unique solution of DE (1) which
satisfies initial conditions

                           y(x0) = y0, y ′(x0) = y1, ..., y (n−1)(x0) = yn−1,                         (2)

where y0, ..., yn−1 and x0 are given constants. A problem consisting of the DE (1) together with the
initial conditions (2) is called an initial-value problem or the Cauchy problem.





Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 15, 2026                 3 / 53

DEFINITION 1.
If f1, f2, ..., fm are m given functions, and c1, c2, ..., cm are m constants, then the expression

                                            c1f1 + c2f2 + ... + cmfm

is called a linear combination of f1, f2, ..., fm.
EXAMPLE
A linear combination of functions sin(x), cos(x)  is

                                      c1 sin(x) + c2 cos(x), c1, c2 ∈R.

 THEOREM 1.  Any linear combination of solutions of the linear homogeneous differential equation (1)
is also a solution of (1).
Proof.
Let y1, y2, . . . , ym be solutions of (1) on the interval I. Then for each i = 1, 2, . . . , m,

                a0(x)y i(n) (x) + a1(x)y i(n−1) (x) + · · · + an−1(x)y i′ (x) + an(x)yi(x) = 0

for all x ∈I.




Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 15, 2026                 4 / 53

Take an arbitrary linear combination:

                           y(x) = c1y1(x) + c2y2(x) + · · · + cmym(x),

where c1, c2, . . . , cm are constants.
Since differentiation is a linear operation, for each k = 0, 1, . . . , n,

                        y (k)(x) = c1y 1(k) (x) + c2y 2(k) (x) + · · · + cmy m(k) (x).

Substitute y and its derivatives into the left-hand side of (1), then interchange the order of summation
and factor out the constants ci:

      a0(x)y (n)(x) + a1(x)y (n−1)(x) + · · · + an−1(x)y ′(x) + an(x)y(x)
           m              m                      m             m
    = a0(x) X ciy i(n) (x) + a1(x) X ciy i(n−1) (x) + · · · + an−1(x) X ciy i′ (x) + an(x) X ciyi(x)
                i=1                   i=1                              i=1                  i=1
       m
    = X ci h a0(x)y i(n) (x) + a1(x)y i(n−1) (x) + · · · + an−1(x)y i′ (x) + an(x)yi(x)i .
          i=1





Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 15, 2026                 5 / 53

Since each yi is a solution of (1), the expression in square brackets is identically zero:

                a0(x)y i(n) (x) + a1(x)y i(n−1) (x) + · · · + an−1(x)y i′ (x) + an(x)yi(x) = 0

for every x ∈I and for each i = 1, 2, . . . , m.
Therefore,
                  a0(x)y (n)(x) + a1(x)y (n−1)(x) + · · · + an−1(x)y ′(x) + an(x)y(x)
                 m
           = X ci · 0 = 0
                        i=1

for all x ∈I. Theorem is proved.

DEFINITION 2.
The n functions f1(x), f2(x), ..., fn(x) are called linearly dependent on I, if there exist constants
c1, c2, ..., cn, not all zero, such that

                                  c1f1(x) + c2f2(x) + ... + cnfn(x) = 0

for all x ∈I.
EXAMPLE
Whether or not functions x and 2x are linearly dependent on I = R?
We prove that x and 2x are linearly dependent on R. Indeed, there exist constants c1 and c2, not both
zero, such that
                                         c1x + c2(2x) = 0
for all x ∈R. For example, let c1 = 2 and c2 = −1.
DEFINITION 3.
The n functions f1(x), f2(x), ..., fn(x) are called linearly independent on I, if they are not linearly
dependent there. That is, the functions f1(x), f2(x), ..., fn(x) are linearly independent on I, if the relation

                                  c1f1(x) + c2f2(x) + ... + cnfn(x) = 0

for all x ∈I implies that
                                          c1 = c2 = ... = cn = 0.


Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 15, 2026                 7 / 53

EXAMPLE
Whether or not functions x and x2 are linearly independent on I = R?
We assert that x and x2 are linearly independent on R, since

                                          c1x + c2x2 = 0

for all x implies that both c1 = 0 and c2 = 0. We may verify this in the following way. We differentiate
both sides of c1x + c2x2 = 0 to obtain c1 + 2c2x = 0, which must also hold for all x. Then from this we
also have c1x + 2c2x2 = 0, for all such x. Thus we have both

                        c1x + c2x2 = 0   and  c1x + 2c2x2 = 0  for all  x.                      (3)

Subtracting the first from the second gives c2x2 = 0 for all x, which at once implies c2 = 0. Then from
(3) we conclude that c1x = 0 for all x. Obviously, c1 = 0.





Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 15, 2026                 8 / 53

DEFINITION 4.
The Wronskian of the differentiable functions y1(x), y2(x), ..., yn(x) is the function

                                                 y1       y2       . . .    yn
                                            y 1′      y 2′       . . .    y n′
                     W(y1, y2, ..., yn) =                        ...                                    ...                            ...                            ...        .
                                           y 1(n−1)  y 2(n−1)    . . .  y n(n−1)

In order to determine whether or not some functions or solutions of linear DE (1) are linearly
independent we will use the following theorem.
THEOREM 2.
If f1(x), f2(x), ..., fn(x) are linearly dependent on an interval I, then W (f1, f2, ..., fn)(x) = 0 for all x ∈I.
If W (f1, f2, ..., fn)(x0) ̸= 0 for some x0 ∈I, then f1(x), f2(x), ..., fn(x) are linearly independent on an
interval I.





Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 15, 2026                 9 / 53

EXAMPLE
DE
                                       y ′′ −2y ′ + y = 0

has the solutions y1(x) = exp(x) and y2(x) = x exp(x). Whether or not these solutions are linearly
independent on R?
Since both functions y1(x) and y2(x) are solutions of linear DE we can use Theorem 2 and calculate the
Wronskian

                                exp(x)      x exp(x)
        W(exp(x), x exp(x)) =                 = exp(x)(x exp(x) + exp(x))−
                                exp(x)  x exp(x) + exp(x)

                          −x exp(2x) = exp(2x) ̸= 0.





Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 15, 2026                10 / 53

Thus y1(x) and y2(x) are linearly independent on R.
THEOREM 3.

The n-th order linear homogeneous differential equation

                 a0(x)y (n)(x) + a1(x)y (n−1)(x) + ... + an−1(x)y ′(x) + an(x)y(x) = 0               (4)

always possesses n solutions that are linearly independent. Further, if f1(x), f2(x), ..., fn(x) are n linearly
independent solutions of (4) on I, then every solution g of (4) on I can be expressed as a linear
combination
                            g(x) = c1f1(x) + c2f2(x) + ... + cnfn(x)

of these n linearly independent solutions by proper choice of the constants c1, c2, ..., cn. The function
g(x) with arbitrary constants c1, c2, ..., cn is a solution of (4).





Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 15, 2026                11 / 53

From Theorem 3 we conclude that any set of n linearly independent solutions of n-th order linear
homogeneous differential equation (4) on I  is a basis for the solutions of this equation on I.

DEFINITION 5.
Any set y1, y2, ..., yn of n linearly independent solutions of the linear homogeneous n-th order differential
equation (4) on an interval I  is said to be a fundamental set of solutions on the interval I.
If y1, y2, ..., yn constitute a fundamental set of solutions of the linear homogeneous n-th order differential
equation (4) on an interval I, then the set of all solutions of (4) on I can be expressed as a linear
combination
                              y = c1y1(x) + c2y2(x) + ... + cnyn(x),

where c1, c2, ..., cn are arbitrary constants.

EXAMPLE.
Show that the functions y1 = exp t and y2 = exp(−2t) are a fundamental set of solutions to the
equation
                              L(y) ≡y ′′ + y ′ −2y = 0   on   R.                              (5)

Find the general solution of (5).





Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 15, 2026                12 / 53

We first show that y1 = exp t and y2 = exp(−2t) are solutions to the equation (5):

                             L(exp t) = exp t + exp t −2 exp t = 0,

                    L(exp(−2t)) = 4 exp(−2t) −2 exp(−2t) −2 exp(−2t) = 0.

To prove that y1 and y2 are linearly independent we use Theorem 2 and calculate the Wronskian

                             exp t    exp(−2t)
      W(exp t, exp(−2t)) =              = −2 exp(−t) −exp(−t) = −3 exp(−t).
                             exp t  −2 exp(−2t)

Since W (exp t, exp(−2t)) ̸= 0 we conclude that y1 and y2 are a fundamental set of solutions to the DE
(5) on R. Then the general solution of the equation on R is

                                   y = c1 exp t + c2 exp(−2t),

 where c1, c2 are arbitrary constants.





Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 15, 2026                13 / 53

REMARK.
A fundamental set of solutions to the equation above is not unique. Moreover, there are infinitely many
fundamental sets of solutions. For example, y1 = c1 exp t and y2 = c2 exp(−2t), where c1, c2 ̸= 0.
Indeed, both functions satisfy DE (5) and

                                     c1 exp t    c2 exp(−2t)
     W(c1 exp t, c2 exp(−2t)) =                = −2c1c2 exp(−t) −c1c2 exp(−t)
                                     c1 exp t  −2c2 exp(−2t)

                      = −3c1c2 exp(−t) ̸= 0.

There are another fundamental sets of solutions.

Linear nonhomogeneous differential equation of order n.

We will consider linear nonhomogeneous differential equation of order n

               a0(x)y (n)(x) + a1(x)y (n−1)(x) + ... + an−1(x)y ′(x) + an(x)y(x) = f (x),             (6)

where a0, a1, ..., an and f are continuous functions on interval I and that a0(x) ̸= 0 for any x ∈I.

DEFINITION 6.
The linear homogeneous differential equation of order n

                 a0(x)y (n)(x) + a1(x)y (n−1)(x) + ... + an−1(x)y ′(x) + an(x)y(x) = 0               (7)

is called corresponding to linear nonhomogeneous differential equation (6).
From Existence and uniqueness theorem1 it follows that there exists a unique solution of DE (6) which
satisfies initial conditions

                           y(x0) = y0, y ′(x0) = y1, ..., y (n−1)(x0) = yn−1,                         (8)

where y0, ..., yn−1 and x0 are given constants. A problem consisting of the DE (6) together with the
initial conditions (8) is called an initial-value problem or the Cauchy problem.
   1See Lecture 1

Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 15, 2026                15 / 53

THEOREM 4.
Let yp be a particular solution of linear nonhomogeneous differential equation (6) and y1, y2, ..., yn be a
fundamental set of solutions of linear homogeneous differential equation (7) corresponding to (6). Then
every solution y of the n-th order nonhomogeneous equation (6) can be expressed in the form

                          y(x) = c1y1(x) + c2y2(x) + ... + cnyn(x) + yp                          (9)

for suitable choice of the constants c1, c2, ..., cn. The function y with arbitrary constants c1, c2, ..., cn is a
solution of (6).





Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 15, 2026                16 / 53

Method of variation of parameters

By Theorem 4 we could find all solutions of linear nonhomogeneous differential equation (6) if we know
a fundamental set of solutions of corresponding to (6) linear homogeneous DE (7) and a particular
solution of (6). To obtain a particular solution we can use the method of variation of parameters
(Lagrange method). For the simplicity we demonstrate this method for the second order linear
nonhomogeneous DE
                             y ′′(x) + a1(x)y ′(x) + a2(x)y(x) = f (x),                          (10)

where a1, a2 and f are continuous functions on interval I. Suppose we know a fundamental set of
solutions y1, y2 for corresponding to (10) linear homogeneous DE. Then

                              y(x) = c1y1(x) + c2y2(x), c1, c2 ∈R

is a general solution of this homogeneous DE on I. Such a function y can not be a solution of (10)
unless f (x) ≡0. However, suppose we allow c1, c2 to become functions of x and then ask whether there
is a solution of (10) on interval I of the form

and find the derivatives of yp :

                          y p′ = c′1y1 + c1y 1′ + c′2y2 + c2y 2′ = c1y 1′ + c2y 2,′

                                y p′′ = c′1y 1′ + c1y 1′′ + c′2y 2′ + c2y 2′′ .

THEOREM 5.
Let f be continuous function on an interval I. Every solution y of (10) on I can be written as

                           y(x) = c1y1(x) + c2y2(x) + yp, c1, c2 ∈R                         (15)

where yp is a particular solution of (10) and two functions y1, y2 are a fundamental set of solutions of
corresponding to (10) linear homogeneous differential equation. A particular solution yp is given by
(11), (14).
